name: Each Platform Has Fatal Flaws
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Why More Money Might Not Fix Any of This
lesson.summary: Every qubit platform has at least one problem that looks less like a manufacturing hurdle and more like a genuine physics limit, and telling the two apart is the real test of quantum computing skepticism.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter compared five platforms across several axes and found no clean winner. This chapter asks a sharper question: for each platform, is its biggest weakness the kind of problem that more engineering effort and more money reliably fix, the way classical chip manufacturers have spent seventy years shrinking transistors, or is it the kind of problem that bumps against an actual limit in the underlying physics, one that no amount of investment straightforwardly solves? That distinction, the engineering versus physics barrier, is the right lens for evaluating each platform's flaws rather than dismissing all of quantum computing as equally hopeless or equally promising.

Superconducting qubits face a wiring bottleneck: every additional qubit needs its own control and readout lines running from room temperature electronics down through a dilution refrigerator, and those lines carry heat as well as signal. Some of this is genuinely an engineering problem, and real progress has come from multiplexing signals and moving some control electronics into the cold stages of the fridge. But part of it runs into real physics: the materials used to build the circuits contain microscopic defects, so called two level systems in oxide layers, that cause decoherence in ways researchers have not been able to fully eliminate despite two decades of concerted materials science effort, suggesting at least part of this limitation is closer to a physics problem than a pure manufacturing one.

Trapped ions face a different ceiling. Laser driven gates have an intrinsic speed limit set by the physics of atomic transitions, so operations will likely always be slower per gate than electrical circuit based platforms, a genuine physics constraint rather than an engineering shortfall. Scaling beyond a single trap requires either shuttling ions between physically separate zones or linking modules with photonic connections, both active engineering problems, but both currently add error and complexity every time they are attempted at larger scale.

Photonic systems carry perhaps the starkest example of a physics level flaw: there is no good way to store a photon while other operations happen, because a stationary photon is close to a contradiction, and two qubit gates between photons remain either probabilistic or dependent on nonlinear effects that are inherently weak in ordinary materials. Neutral atoms face a built in lifetime limit on the Rydberg states their gates depend on, which puts a practical ceiling on how many sequential operations can happen before an atom's excited state simply decays. And topological qubits face the most basic flaw of all: it remains genuinely unsettled whether the physics they depend on, robust non-abelian anyons with true topological protection, exists in a controllable, scalable form outside of theory, as the retracted 2018 Majorana claim and the skepticism around Microsoft's 2025 announcement both illustrate.

None of this means quantum computing is a dead end. It means the qubits are extremely fragile problem does not have one universal solution, and every proposed fix trades one limitation for another that has not yet been proven fixable at scale. A skeptic's job here is not to declare the whole enterprise impossible, but to keep asking, for each specific claimed breakthrough, whether it addresses a genuine physics constraint or merely an engineering inconvenience that better funding will eventually smooth over.
